newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - U.S. refinery margins seen on downtrend.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - U.S. refinery margins seen on downtrend.

text.p: U.S. refinery margins hit an early peak this year and are likely to remain in a downtrend for the next several months, according to analysts.
The strong rally in gasoline prices that occurred in February/March meant refinery margins hit what analysts expect will be the peak of the year more than a month before they were expected to.
Every year since the Gulf War, margins have peaked in late April or May as gasoline inventories were built up ahead of the Memorial Day weekend and the start of the summer "driving season."
"Refinery margins peaked in mid-April and they are on their way down," said Ken Miller, senior principal at Houston consultancy Purvin & Gertz.

Though refining margins nationwide rose to $4.22 a barrel in the week ended May 24 from the previous week's level of $3.77, the May average has been $4.01 compared with April's $4.67, according to Paul Ting, analyst with Salomon Brothers Inc.

"Margins have collapsed everywhere, particularly because of the early strength in gasoline. The rally occurred a little bit early this year because of the later refinery (maintenance) turnarounds late last year," said Miller.
The highest level in gasoline futures on NYMEX this spring occurred in March at 69.00 cents a barrel. Last year, the spring peak was April 29's $78.10, a post-Gulf War high.

Regionally, West and East Coast refineries have seen the biggest slump in their margins. West Coast (excluding California) plant margins were down to $1.99 a barrel in the week ended May 24 from the previous week's $2.43 level and the May average has sunk to $2.73 a barrel from April's $5.96, according to Ting.
"There has been a high increase of gasoline stocks over the last three to four weeks in the West Coast and demand has not been that good," said Miller.
The mediocre East Coast margins appeared more a factor of unseasonally cold spring weather than inventory.

"Margins are not very good for the East Coast," said Amoco Corp economist Ted Eck. "I thought demand would have been stronger for the region. But I think the cold weather has been a major consideration" in holding back demand.

According to Ting, East Coast products factories made a slight gain in the week ended May 24 to $3.77 a barrel from $3.36. But the May average is still about $3.61 compared to the April average of $4.13.
"The pressure is on to improve margins by cutting costs. That is the drive behind all the recent mergers," said Eck. "People have already done the obvious stuff."
